title: Guru Har Rai: gentleness
hookLine: the seventh Guru's light: walk gently, heal whoever asks
tomorrow: a Guru who was a child, in a city full of sickness. what did he do?

cards: Some people move through a crowded room and nothing gets knocked over: not a cup, not a feeling. Here's an odd detail. Tradition says Guru Hargobind's grandson, Har Rai, kept horsemen, like his grandfather.

Yet the story people tell about him is about a flower. As a boy, walking in a garden, his wide robe caught a flower and broke it. His grandfather told him: if you wear a robe like that, carry it carefully.
From then on, the story goes, he gathered his robe close every time he walked.

teach.h: A GURU WITH HORSEMEN, AND A FLOWER.
teach.b: So why is a Guru with horsemen remembered for a flower? A second odd detail explains the first.

teach.h: MEDICINE FOR AN OLD ENEMY'S SON.
teach.b: Tradition says Guru Har Rai kept a store of herbs and medicines, and when Dara Shikoh, a son of the emperor Shah Jahan, fell badly ill, the medicine that helped came from the Guru's store.
The emperor's armies had fought Guru Hargobind. The medicine went anyway. Gentleness here isn't weakness.
It's strength that gathers its robe so it doesn't break what it passes. And it heals whoever asks, even the house of an old enemy.
The Guru Granth Sahib keeps a line for this from Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi whose verses are in the Sikh scripture, on Ang 1382.
In paraphrase: answer evil with goodness; don't let anger fill your mind. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh scripture's line about repaying harm with goodness comes from a Muslim saint.
Simran's version this week, back at her dad's dispatch desk for the summer: the dispatcher who snapped at her on her first day calls in, panicked. His kid is sick, and his route list needs covering.
She stays late and covers it.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai for his gentleness and his care for the sick; many gurdwaras and Sikh groups today run free clinics, medical camps and care for the sick as seva.

o: the child Guru who nursed the sick in Delhi's epidemic
the Guru who built the Akal Takht facing the temple
the seventh Guru, gentle enough to heal an enemy's son

games.q: the seventh Guru — tap the pairs.
p: gathered close after a broken flower
the emperor's son who got the medicine
herbs and medicines for whoever asks

s: gentleness means being too soft to stand up for anything
Har Rai kept horsemen; his gentleness was strength that gathers its robe.
a verse by a Muslim Sufi, Sheikh Farid, is in the Guru Granth Sahib
Ang 1382: answer evil with goodness; don't let anger fill your mind.
tradition says Guru Har Rai refused to help the emperor's family
the story is the opposite: the medicine went to Dara Shikoh.

games.q: a classmate who trashed you online last month missed a week sick and asks to borrow your notes. what fits Guru Har Rai?
o: send the notes, no lecture; gentleness heals whoever asks.
send them, but only after he apologizes, so it's fair.
say no politely; gentleness means avoiding trouble, not inviting it.
games.why: the Guru's medicine went to the son of an emperor whose armies fought his grandfather. Farid: answer evil with goodness.

practice: Stand and walk slowly across the room and back, as quietly as you can, heel then toe. Keep your arms close, the way Har Rai gathered his robe, and notice what you'd usually brush past: a door, a chair, a cord.
Turn, and walk it again, softer still.

wordCard.voice: Guru Har Rai: the seventh Guru, whose light is gentleness. He gathered his robe for a flower, and sent medicine to an old enemy's son.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: daya, compassion; the gentleness that heals whoever asks.

carryVoice: Here's the line: gentleness, a robe gathered close and healing for whoever asks. Softly, then.
